papers.title: Mechanism-Level Chemical Reaction Simulation with Electron Bookkeeping Transformer
papers.abstract: Modeling chemical reaction mechanisms is central to understanding and predicting chemical reactivity. We present Electron Bookkeeping Transformer (Bookkeeper), a data-driven model that simulates chemical reactions at mechanistic resolution by generating electron movement trajectories. Following the symbolic arrow-pushing formalism in chemistry, Bookkeeper explicitly models each electron as a token and predicts its movement sequentially, ensuring mass and charge conservation during both elementary step and reaction pathway predictions by construction. On reaction-size-balanced test sets, Bookkeeper improves top-1 elementary-step accuracy, top-1 pathway rank accuracy, and top-1 to top-5 product prediction accuracy over FlowER. On the entire test set, it achieves higher elementary-step top-1 accuracy but lower pathway accuracy than FlowER. Bookkeeper also samples elementary steps substantially faster, adapts to several unseen reaction types with minimal fine-tuning, and generates candidate chemical transformations for further screening. These results suggest that explicit electron bookkeeping is a useful framework for virtually screening chemical reactions across diverse reagents, validating computer-assisted synthesis planning predictions, and providing mechanistic interpretations of reactivity.

papers.title: Confident and Wrong: Structure Confidence Is a Poor Selection Filter for Protein Function
papers.abstract: Structure-guided protein design can generate plausible candidates, but structural confidence does not predict function. We trained a function-guided model on measured metal-binding affinity with protein sequence, ligand identity, and assay conditions, and used it to design rare earth element (REE) binding variants of lanmodulin, a lanthanide-binding protein with four EF-hand domains. We screened 297 designs from three strategies against terbium and dysprosium, adjacent lanthanides among the hardest REE pairs to separate. Selection on structural confidence inverted the outcome it was meant to improve. The Structure-Confidence-Selected panel carried the highest pTM, complex ipLDDT, and composite confidence scores, and expressed at 97%, yet only 16.7% of its designs bound terbium (95% CI 10.4 to 25.7), against 83.3% (74.6 to 89.5) for the function-guided panel, whose confidence scores were the lowest. The odds of binding differed 25-fold between the two panels (Fisher exact $p = 1 \times 10^{-20}$). No structural-confidence metric separated binders from non-binders consistently across panels, whereas the function-trained model's predicted pKd gave the highest ROC AUC in every panel, 0.79 to 0.92, and ranked measured affinity among function-guided binders at Spearman $\rho = 0.98$. On the design objective, Tb/Dy selectivity, the function-guided designs also exceeded the natural lanmodulin family, outranking a randomly drawn ortholog 84% of the time across 149 orthologs. Structural confidence is a plausibility signal, not a selection criterion for function; direct supervision on measured function is what ranks designs.

papers.title: Deciphering multiple binding modes in large protein complexes via Enhanced Sampling and beta-VAE: the CYFIP1-eIF4E case
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) drives cap-dependent translation, regulated by 4E-binding proteins (4E-BPs) competing for its dorsal and lateral surfaces. CYFIP1, a scaffold protein, is both a WAVE Regulatory Complex component and a non-canonical 4E-BP repressing translation via a short helical motif, linked to autism spectrum disorders and cancer. Prior work modeled only this isolated motif as a peptide, leaving the full interface uncharacterized. Starting from this preliminary evidence, we modeled the full-length proteins as flexible partners: all-atom simulations fed a data-driven docking search (HADDOCK3), which guided funnel-restrained Temperature-Accelerated Molecular Dynamics of a coarse-grained Martini 3 representation. Ten replicas accumulated 100 $\mu$s of enhanced sampling. Funnel-restraint variables efficiently sample binding and unbinding but are structurally degenerate: direct clustering of the raw trajectory collapses these poses into poorly resolved groups. We instead reweighted the biased trajectories onto a contact-based latent space built by benchmarking PCA against a beta-Variational Autoencoder, then clustered minima of the equilibrium free-energy surface: only intermediate regularization resolved distinct, homogeneous modes. Three such modes recur, engaging eIF4E's canonical dorsal site, its non-canonical lateral site, and both. We find that CYFIP1 also engages eIF4E through a second surface, the same that mediates its WAVE-complex dimerization, and a basic patch. Both plausibly explain residual binding previously reported after motif mutation. This suggests its translational and cytoskeletal roles compete for the same surface. Most contacts on eIF4E fall outside this dorsal/lateral interface. This heterogeneous, plastic ensemble offers a structural basis for mutagenesis and therapeutic peptide design.

papers.title: CARVE: A glycan-specific framework for assessing protein-glycan binding-pose quality
papers.abstract: Protein-glycan interactions depend on the precise three-dimensional arrangement of carbohydrates at protein-binding interfaces, yet reliable assessment of predicted complex structures remains challenging. Existing evaluations commonly rely on fixed root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) thresholds, which do not fully account for the structural diversity and conformational flexibility of glycans. Here we developed CARVE, a glycan-specific framework for evaluating protein-glycan structure predictions. Through topology-aware glycan parsing, CARVE integrates orientation RMSD (oRMSD), interface-ring RMSD (irRMSD) and the fraction of native contacts (Fnat) to assess glycan scaffold geometry, interface-ring placement and native-contact recovery. These descriptors define four quality categories (CARVE-Level) with geometric thresholds that scale with the degree of polymerization (DP), and a continuous CARVE-Score, which reproduced those categories on 25,068 independently generated poses without recalibration (macro-F1 = 0.892). Pairing these measures with glycan-specific topological, chemical and geometric validity checks, we benchmarked nine prediction methods on CARVE-Bench, comprising 1,974 experimentally determined protein-glycan complexes. Among the top 25 predictions per target, HADDOCK3 achieved the highest Acceptable-level success rate (47.0%), whereas no method produced a high-quality, structurally valid pose for more than one in five. Collectively, CARVE provides a standardized basis for assessing protein-glycan structure prediction methods and guiding the development of more accurate docking and co-folding approaches.

papers.title: Monroe: A Molecular Foundation Model for In-Context Probabilistic Inference
papers.abstract: Bioassay activity prediction is often data-limited because drug-discovery datasets rely on time-consuming and expensive wet-lab experiments for data generation and evaluation. This challenge has inspired recent research into molecular foundation models (MFMs), which aim to encode general-purpose chemical knowledge into molecular representations that generalize well in data-constrained scenarios. This paper presents Monroe, a new MFM with several innovations over the existing state of the art: increased scale allowing pre-training on over 81 million molecules from the PM6 quantum chemistry dataset; improved graph representation of stereochemistry; improved training losses including conformer denoising and embedding decorrelation; improved multi-task learning; and the use of a prior-data-fitted model (TabPFNv3) for downstream in-context prediction. Our evaluations use a principled pairwise comparison framework that measures statistically significant performance differences. Across established Polaris benchmarks, Monroe matches or exceeds existing MFMs, while on activity cliff benchmarks, designed to assess utility for molecular discovery, it achieves significant improvements over prior methods. Finally, ablation and transfer experiments show that PFN-based downstream predictors also substantially improve two leading existing models, MiniMol and CheMeleon, yielding new state-of-the-art variants we call MiniMol_PFN and CheMeleon_PFN, suggesting that our downstream adaptation strategy generalizes beyond Monroe. Source code is at github.com/blazejba/Monroe

papers.title: Learning Task-Specific Antibody Representations via Function-Aware Masking
papers.abstract: Antibody-specific language models pretrained via masked language modeling (MLM) learn representations that are critical for downstream sequence design and property prediction tasks. Yet, the corruption process itself is rarely leveraged as a source of inductive bias during pretraining. While preferentially masking complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) improves binding-related predictions, antibodies possess diverse biological priors over a variety of functions. Herein, we introduce function-aware masking, a family of pretraining algorithms that align mask placement with specific functional priors (e.g., from IMGT annotations or structure predictions) to shape the learned representation space. We show that these specialist masking strategies significantly improve performance on their respective objectives, yielding up to a 14% gain on structure-related tasks and up to a 5.9x improvement on CDR-related tasks. To further improve performance across multiple functional axes, we develop hybrid masking strategies that integrate multiple priors, balancing reconstruction over binding, structural, and biophysical objectives. Our results demonstrate that informed mask placement provides a parameter-free mechanism for imposing functional inductive biases in antibody language model training.
